name: Animal Health, Disease & Biosecurity

objectives.text: Identify signs that an animal is healthy versus signs that it may be sick, such as bright eyes, normal appetite, droopy posture, or coughing
Explain why washing hands and changing clothes after handling animals helps keep both people and animals healthy
Describe simple daily care practices that prevent illness in animals, such as clean pens, fresh water, dry shelter, and watching animals for changes
Explain how germs can travel between animals through direct contact, air, water, insects, people, and shared equipment
Classify common livestock diseases as caused by bacteria, viruses, fungi, parasites, or noninfectious factors
Describe the life cycle of a common internal or external livestock parasite and identify the stage where control measures can break the cycle
Apply biosecurity practices for exhibiting animals at fairs and shows, including health papers, avoiding shared equipment, and isolating animals when they return home
Investigate how a specific livestock disease spreads and identify the biosecurity practices that limit its transmission
Explain how vaccination protects individual animals and a whole herd or flock and why following a vaccination schedule matters
Identify the characteristics of causal agents and vectors of animal diseases, such as ticks, flies, mosquitoes, rodents, and wild birds
Summarize the characteristics of wounds, common diseases, parasites, and physiological disorders in a major livestock species
Explain methods of determining animal health, including visual observation, vital signs, body condition, and laboratory tests such as fecal egg counts
Summarize the importance of biosecurity to the animal industry at the local, state, national, and global levels
Create a health record system for an SAE animal project that tracks observations, vaccinations, deworming, and treatments
Analyze a set of livestock symptoms against a reference chart to identify the most likely illness or disorder and an appropriate response
Determine when an animal health concern needs to be referred to a veterinarian or other animal health professional
Analyze the health risk of common zoonotic diseases to humans and identify methods to prevent their transmission
Analyze local, state, and national biosecurity procedures such as premises identification, animal disease traceability, interstate health certificates, and foreign animal disease response
Analyze herd or flock health data to evaluate how well preventive measures are controlling the spread of diseases, parasites, and disorders
Explain how overuse or misuse of antibiotics and dewormers leads to resistance and describe judicious use practices that slow it
Evaluate the economic and trade impact of a major animal disease outbreak, such as highly pathogenic avian influenza or African swine fever, on producers and the industry
Design a herd or flock health maintenance and disease prevention plan that includes vaccination, parasite control, and monitoring for a natural or confined environment
Design a biosecurity plan for an animal operation that addresses quarantine, sanitation, traffic control, pest control, and recordkeeping

changes: I kept all six original competencies. Two were reworded: the grade 4 objective now leaves out feeding, which belongs to Animal Nutrition & Feed Science, and the grade 10 diagnosis objective is now framed as analysis. I changed the grade 6 classification so it no longer centers nutritional deficiency, keeping it on disease causes. I added early hygiene and zoonosis awareness at grade 3 and disease transmission routes at grade 5. I added parasite life cycles and fair and show biosecurity in the middle grades, and vaccination and herd immunity at grade 8. For grades 9 to 12 I added objectives tied to the standards: causal agents and vectors, characteristics of diseases and disorders, health assessment methods, biosecurity importance across levels, referral decisions, zoonotic risk, regulatory biosecurity procedures, and analysis of prevention data. I also added an SAE health record system, antimicrobial resistance, and the economic impact of outbreaks. Treatment administration and welfare were left out because they belong to Veterinary Practices & Animal Welfare.
